title: Structural Insights into Antibody-based Inhibition of the Angiotensin Receptor
content: The angiotensin II type I receptor (AT1R), a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that regulates cardiac and renal function, is one of the most successful pharmaceutical targets for the treatment of high blood pressure. Small molecule AT1R inhibitors are well-tolerated in most individuals, but are contraindicated during pregnancy, as they cross the placenta and exhibit severe on-target fetal toxicity. Alternative strategies to target AT1R could provide new avenues to treat hypertensive disorders during pregnancy, such as preeclampsia, a leading cause of maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. High subtype specificity and differing tissue distribution make antibodies intriguing alternatives to small molecules for therapeutically targeting GPCRs, but the mechanisms by which antibodies modulate GPCR function are not well understood [1].
